title: Astrid and the Drop
premise: Tamsin Thackeray, a sleepless interpreter haunted by the 'incident' at the Geneva talks, receives a calendar invitation from his handler, Elias Voss—sent three days after Voss's body was pulled from the lake. Following the dead man's breadcrumbs, Tamsin uncovers a plot to destroy the peace delegation's final summit and stage it as an infrastructure accident, implicating the very faction he once protected. As he races through a web of compromised officials, he must choose between loyalty to the service that made him invisible and the truth that could save hundreds. In the end, Tamsin exposes the attack at the cost of his own cover, testifying from hiding as justice outside the law—and finds, for the first time in a year, he can sleep.
about_author: A. M. Okafor is the pen name of a former conference interpreter who spent a decade behind the glass of international negotiations before turning to fiction. They write thrillers about the people history forgets—the translators, couriers, and fixers who hear everything and are heard by no one.

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.summary: Tamsin Thackeray, running on four hours' broken sleep, translates a routine briefing for the faltering peace delegation when his phone buzzes: a meeting request from Elias Voss, his handler—dead for three days. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into morbid curiosity; the first crack in his carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Lake Kept
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present-day insomnia: the 'incident' at the Geneva annex, a misheard phrase Tamsin translated under pressure, and Voss telling him to forget it. Now Tamsin visits the lakeside spot where Voss drowned. POV Tamsin with Voss flashback. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing; the past refusing to stay translated away.

chapters.title: Dead Man's Calendar
chapters.summary: Tamsin accepts the meeting invite against every instinct. The location resolves to a decommissioned tram depot; attached is a single encrypted line only Voss would know how to phrase. His apartment shows signs of a search—not burglars, professionals. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: fear curdling into resolve; someone wants him watched or gone.

chapters.title: The Depot
chapters.summary: At the depot Tamsin finds no ghost—only a dead-drop cache Voss prepared before dying: a burner phone, a keycard, and a note reading 'You heard it right the first time.' A watcher tails him out; Tamsin loses them in the old freight tunnels. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: vertigo of purpose—after a year of erasure, he has a task again.

chapters.title: Interpreter's Ear
chapters.summary: Back at the delegation, Tamsin works the summit prep sessions while secretly replaying what he truly heard during the incident: not a threat, a schedule. Cross-referencing delegate itineraries, he realizes the final plenary at the Kessler Hall falls on an anniversary someone cares about. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: the interpreter's curse turned weapon—hearing what others mean, not say.

chapters.title: Deputy Director Reyes
chapters.summary: Tamsin's service superior, Deputy Director Reyes, summons him with unsettling warmth, probing whether Voss left anything behind. Tamsin lies well—for an interpreter. Leaving, he spots Reyes's aide photographing his building. POV alternating Tamsin and a cold, controlled Reyes. Emotional beat: the realization that the institution itself may be the predator.

chapters.title: Nadia
chapters.summary: Tamsin turns to Nadia Ferro, a delegation security liaison and the one person he almost let himself love before the incident froze him. He gives her half the truth; she gives him access logs showing Kessler Hall's maintenance contractor was swapped two weeks ago. POV Nadia, then Tamsin. Emotional beat: tenderness rekindling under operational distrust—love against duty begins its argument.

chapters.title: The Contractor
chapters.summary: Following the shell company, Tamsin finds the 'maintenance crew' are ex-military logistics men moving crates of industrial solvent into the hall's sub-basement—enough to bring the floor down during the plenary, blamed on aging infrastructure. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: horror crystallizing into clarity; the accident has a blueprint.

chapters.title: Voss's Voice
chapters.summary: The burner phone rings. A synthesized voice built from Voss's intercepted calls walks Tamsin through a partial file: Voss discovered the plot, was silenced, and pre-arranged this lifeline—but the file is incomplete without a passphrase Voss never sent. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude tangled; his dead handler still teaching him.

chapters.title: Loyalty Audit
chapters.summary: Reyes suspends Tamsin pending a 'routine loyalty review,' confiscating his credentials—a move designed to isolate him before the summit. Tamsin understands: the review isn't routine, it's containment. POV Reyes and Tamsin. Emotional beat: betrayal landing hard; the service he served is auditing him out of existence.

chapters.title: Safehouse of Strangers
chapters.summary: Off the grid, Tamsin shelters with a retired interpreter, Marta, who once ran Voss's networks and owes him a debt. She decodes part of the file: the attack's trigger is a phrase to be spoken in the plenary's closing translation loop—someone inside the interpretation booth. POV Marta, then Tamsin. Emotional beat: unlikely sanctuary; the community of the invisible protecting its own.

chapters.title: The Inside Booth
chapters.summary: Process of elimination narrows the inside man to three interpreters on the plenary roster. Tamsin risks contact with one, Anselm, who panics and bolts—straight into a car with Reyes's aide. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: guilt reigniting; his tradecraft just got a frightened man taken.

chapters.title: Nadia's Choice
chapters.summary: Nadia confronts Tamsin with what her own agency knows: they've flagged him as a potential attacker, not a whistleblower. She must decide whether to report him or burn her career helping him. She chooses him—handing over the hall's structural schematics. POV Nadia. Emotional beat: love choosing truth over duty, the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Passphrase
chapters.summary: Marta cracks the file's logic: the passphrase is the mistranslated phrase from the incident, corrected. Tamsin speaks it aloud and the full file opens—names, timeline, and proof Reyes greenlit the operation to collapse the talks and justify a harder regime. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: cathartic devastation; the incident was never his failure, it was the plan's first draft.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.summary: With the summit in two days, Tamsin tries legitimate channels—inspector general, foreign liaison—and watches each door close within hours, tipped off from inside. The system cannot be used against its own author. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: despair transmuting into the thriller's core decision: justice outside the law.

chapters.title: Anselm's Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin traces Anselm to a service safehouse and finds him sedated, alive—leverage, not corpse. Reyes wanted him pliable for tomorrow's booth. Tamsin extracts Anselm's confession on tape: the trigger phrase, the timing, the order-giver's voice. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: grim rescue; evidence won at the edge of becoming what he fights.

chapters.title: Booth Duty
chapters.summary: Summit morning. Tamsin uses forged credentials and Nadia's schematics to enter Kessler Hall as a relief interpreter, taking the booth seat where the trigger will be spoken. Below, delegates gather; in the sub-basement, the solvent waits. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: terror held in professional stillness—the interpreter's mask as armor.

chapters.title: The Trigger Phrase
chapters.summary: Mid-plenary, the second interpreter—Reyes's plant—begins steering the translation toward the trigger. Tamsin overrides the feed, substituting clean text, and keys the emergency channel with the evidence file. The plant attacks him in the booth; they struggle live on an open mic. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: white-knuckle climax; words as the battlefield.

chapters.title: Kessler Hall
chapters.summary: Nadia evacuates the hall on a fire pretext as the plant, exposed, tries to detonate manually; security—finally believing—intercepts him in the sub-basement. The floor holds. Reyes slips out during the chaos, but Tamsin anticipated it, waiting at the garage with the recording playing. POV alternating Tamsin and Nadia. Emotional beat: explosive release; the accident that never was.

chapters.title: Reckoning Off the Books
chapters.summary: Reyes offers Tamsin reinstatement, silence, a future—institutional loyalty in exchange for buried truth. Tamsin refuses and releases everything to three jurisdictions at once, forcing justice the law couldn't self-administer. Reyes is arrested by foreign prosecutors, not his own service. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: quiet triumph; loyalty finally aligned with truth instead of against it.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: From a protected location, Tamsin gives formal testimony—the incident reframed, Voss posthumously cleared, Anselm freed. He and Nadia negotiate what they can be to each other now that duty no longer dictates. The delegation collapses anyway, but honestly this time. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: bittersweet settlement; truth costs more than it pays, and pays anyway.

chapters.title: Sleep
chapters.summary: Weeks later, in a small coastal town under a new name, Tamsin unpacks one box: Voss's note, framed. A letter arrives via Marta—an invitation, benign this time, to teach interpreting. That night he sleeps through until dawn, no dreams of water. POV Tamsin. Emotional beat: resolution and grace; the invisible man, visible at last to himself.
